body_markdown:
Completed in 2022, Ramsey Potts’ Porsche 944 Firehawk tribute car is an ’80s showroom-stock dream made reality. As is often the case, the dream was born decades earlier, when Potts managed to secure a press pass to the 1988 IMSA Camel Continental Grand Prix at Watkins Glen. The Porsche 962 and the V-12-powered Jaguar GTP prototypes weren’t what captured his imagination; it was the production-based cars in the supporting Firestone Firehawk street-stock endurance series. That, thought the racing-obsessed 20-year-old, was everything racing should be.


“I had four jobs while I was in college,” says Potts, now a partner and senior car specialist at Broad Arrow Auctions. “Honestly, my college education was a bit pointless, because all I cared about was going racing.”


His first race car wasn’t a car, but a two-stroke sprint kart, and he didn’t even own a trailer to put it in. On weekends in between studying at the University of Pittsburgh, he’d head to the nearest karting track in a 1991 Pontiac Le Mans purchased for him by his dad. The rebadged Daewoo was an “abomination,” he says, but it was brand-new transportation—and it had a big trunk.


“My entire race team was stuffed in the trunk of that car. No one could ride with me. My girlfriend—now, my wife—had to ride separately because the toolbox and all my parts and everything were in the front seat and the back seat.”


Ramsey Potts at 21, “probably having spent $21 to go racing.”


Courtesy Ramsey Potts


“I was the guy that showed up and basically took his kart entirely apart, stuffed it in the trunk of his Pontiac, and then drove it to the racetrack, took it all out, put it back together again, and went racing.”


He kept karting as he made the jump to cars in the early ’90s, racing a Porsche 944 in the Sports Car Club of America’s (SCCA) Improved Touring class. Over the years, he “bounced around” in different cars, including spec Miatas and a spec Neon, occasionally renting rides. For two years, he even dipped a toe into street-stock endurance racing, running some races in Grand-Am Cup in the early 2000s.


His love of endurance racing had solidified when he attended the 1991 24 Hours of Daytona as a spectator. He slept in the bleachers and, when the race was over, slept in the airport in a sleeping bag. Even today, when he can justify better accommodations, Daytona is a race that Potts rarely misses. “It’s a mythical, mythical event for us from that era.”


Camden Thrasher


Camden Thrasher


Camden Thrasher


His fortunes have improved in the thirty-odd years since then. He kept karting for most of them—through a 25-year career in the insurance sector and during his transition into the automotive world as a car specialist at RM Sotheby’s in 2017.


During 2021, in the lull between his tenure at that auction house and his current position at Broad Arrow, he found himself with six “intensely idle” months. “What does a petrolhead do when they have a little bit of money and a whole lot of time? They go and promptly piss it away on a car.”


Camden Thrasher


Camden Thrasher


Or race car, in Potts’ case. He wanted to get into vintage racing, and it didn’t take him two seconds to choose how: He wanted to race an old Firehawk-style car. His friend and colleague Marvin Waters was racing a Porsche 944 Firehawk tribute car in Historic Sports Car Racing (HSR), North America’s premier vintage and historic racing series, which now operates under the International Motor Sports Association (IMSA). Given Potts’ established love for the 944 and for the Firehawk series, the choice was an easy one. He bought a regular, street-going 944 out of a classified ad in the Porsche Club of America for $7500.


Turning a street car into a race car—even to “showroom-stock” specs—is a serious project. Potts sat down with Colin Dougherty and Tom McCarthy at[CDOC Racing](https://www.instagram.com/cdoc.official/) to make a list of everything the car would need, from roll cage to shocks to bushings to a race seat and window net. It was a long list.


Ramsey Potts and Raifun at the 2026 HSR Mitty presented by Hagerty.


Camden Thrasher


Joe Frazar, of[Frazar Sports Car Services](https://www.jfrazarmotorcars.com/our-staff) in Savannah, Georgia, took the car apart and prepped it for its race-car modifications. This was not as simple as mechanical disassembly—stripping out the sound deadening, for instance, required some nasty chemicals and a lot of elbow grease. The process had a few tense moments, even though Frazar is a “very, very dear friend,” says Potts. Frazar was mad that Potts had bought a $7500 street car and was well on his way to spending six figures turning it into a $10,000 race car.


“I think what Joe said to me one day was, ‘You are the biggest dumbass I have ever known. All you’re trying to do is turn this thing into a rainbow farting unicorn.'”


Potts was well aware that he could have gotten into vintage racing for much, much cheaper. In fact, he’s an evangelist for the accessibility of vintage racing: “You can start with a $10,000 old worn-out spec Miata, spend $5000 to make it slightly less worn out, and you can be on track after an inexpensive SCCA racing school.” But when it came to his 944, things were different. “I had a dream, I had a fantasy, and I was willing to write the check to create it.”


Camden Thrasher


Perhaps for that very reason, Potts seized upon Frazar’s comment and, on the spot, named his race car Rainbow Farting Unicorn. “That was a little much to say, so we abbreviated it. We took the ‘ra’ from rainbow, the ‘f’ from farting, and the ‘un’ from unicorn, and we call her Raifun.”


Colin Dougherty and his team at CDOC Racing fabricated a rollcage and put the car back together with all the race-spec upgrades. Potts wanted to follow the Firehawk template exactly, which meant using as many Porsche parts as possible, like upgrading the brakes and oil cooler and oil filter with the respective parts from a 944 Turbo.


Meanwhile, the Porsche specialists at Lindsey Racing in Oklahoma refreshed the engine to Potts’ request, giving the 2.5-liter, naturally aspirated four-cylinder a little more power and a lot more reliability. Thanks to some tweaks and a lighter-weight valvetrain, pistons, flywheel, and clutch, plus a more open exhaust system (a header and straight pipe), the engine makes about 15 additional hp, for a total of about 165. It’s backed by the factory five-speed transmission, which sends power to a Porsche factory limited-slip differential.


Camden Thrasher


The car hit the track for the first time in September of 2022 at Watkins Glen, where Potts’ Firehawk dream was born. “That place is magic. It’s just a super, super special place.”


The Brumos Racing livery was a must-have from the beginning of the project. Potts even got the family’s consent to run it, “which was very satisfying.” Fellow fans of the Brumos team will appreciate his number choice, as well. Brumos cars always raced under #59, and if the team ran a second car, it used either #58 or #60. Potts’ friend and fellow HSR competitor Marvin Waters fields a Firehawk-tribute 944 wearing number #59. In a deferential nod to history and to his friend, Potts chose #58.


Camden Thrasher


He does about six to eight events with the car per year. He can’t praise its reliability enough. “When the engine was delivered to me, rebuilt, it had 50 miles on the odometer. It now has almost 7000. I have not missed—and this is not hyperbole—I have not missed one lap of one session at one racetrack I’ve ever been to, whether testing or racing with my car. Not one single solitary mechanical driveline \[issue\], \[nothing\] that has prevented me from going on the track and completing a session.


“Now, I have completed a session hobbling around because we had a spring unseat itself on a bump at Sebring, because Sebring is awful, but I finished.”


Camden Thrasher


In short, his 944 is “the best race car I have ever had the privilege of sharing the track with.”


The high point of the HSR race calendar, he says, is the Classic 24 Hours of Daytona. “It’s our white whale, it’s our Masters Tournament, it’s our World Series.” In fact, Potts and his 944 are headed to Daytona International Speedway in a few weeks for the 2026 HSR Classic 24 Hour at Daytona. Despite the name of his race car, Potts has no intention of farting around. “Anybody that tells you, ‘Oh, it’s not about where you finish, it’s about the fun you have’ … Yeah, right. That’s a big part of it, but don’t get me wrong: Winning is awesome.”


Come the weekend of November 15, Potts and “Raifun” will be pursuing maximum fun under the Daytona lights, as they do at every track they visit.
